# Annex C (supplementary file): full transcripts of the worked runs

*Supplement to the technical appendix of "Reviewership Made Explicit". Every transcript is reproduced unedited from `runs/`, in run order, followed by the harness outputs of every check. Markdown headings inside the transcripts are moved down three levels so that they nest under the file headings; the text of each file, including all code and harness output, is otherwise exactly as in `runs/`. In these runs Claude stood in for the handling editor and the reviewer (appendix Section 4.0). The base-model pilot (Run 13) is in `runs/13_pilot/` and is summarized in appendix Section 7.9.*

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_01_elicitor_E0.md`

**Best-Self Elicitor, Mode E: questions to the handling editor** (Reviewership v0.1, message `bs:E0`)

Dear Editor,

Before the reviewer sets out their standards, I would like your answers to four short questions. I will turn your answers into the editor brief (`bs:EB`). The brief fills in what you need from this reviewer (PRA.6) and decides which of the reviewer's standards we discuss first. I have seen only the invitation: the title, the abstract and your note. I have not seen the manuscript.

How I refer to the invitation: `inv:abs.sN` means sentence N of the abstract, and `inv:note` means your note. A short answer, or "no view", is fine for any question.

**bs:E1. Main contribution.** In your reading, what does the manuscript claim as its main contribution? The abstract offers several candidates. Please rank them, merge them or replace them:
- `bs:C1` **Theory.** Interoperability standards make IT functions modular, "lowering the effective asset specificity of the hospital–vendor relationship" (`inv:abs.s3`). The model predicts a positive effect that is stronger where uncertainty is high (`inv:abs.s4`).
- `bs:C2` **Empirical regularity.** Modularity "strongly predicts the share of its IT spending that is outsourced" in a panel of 412 hospitals, 2009–2019 (`inv:abs.s5`).
- `bs:C3` **Adjudication between rivals.** Once modularity is in the model, peer adoption "no longer predicts outsourcing" (`inv:abs.s6`). So the results "rule out mimetic isomorphism as a driver of IT outsourcing in this setting" (`inv:abs.s7`).
- `bs:C4` **Reinterpretation.** A practice "often read as institutional fashion is, on closer inspection, economizing" (`inv:abs.s7`).
- `bs:C5` **Priority.** The paper claims to be "the first study to adjudicate directly between transaction-cost and institutional explanations of IT outsourcing" (`inv:abs.s8`).

Why I ask: each candidate is judged by different standards. C1 is judged by standards for theory and derivation. C2 and C3 are judged by standards for causal identification and evidence. C5 is judged by checking it against the literature. Your ranking decides which dimension the reviewer and I take first.

**bs:E2. Why this reviewer.** Your note asks for their reading of "the transaction-cost model and the empirical design" (`inv:note`). Which expertise is that, and how deep do you want them to go?
- Possible areas: transaction-cost theory; formal modelling; identification in panel data; institutional theory; the hospital IT setting.
- Possible depth: re-derive the model's predictions (including the uncertainty interaction); re-run the analyses from code and data, if they are supplied; spot-check the reported numbers; or a reasoned reading.

If other reviewers cover some of these areas, for example the institutional side, please say which. That tells me where this reviewer is expected to carry the weight.

**bs:E3. Your concerns.** Do you have concerns or open questions of your own about the manuscript? Your note says "The paper makes strong claims against the institutional account" (`inv:note`).
- If you have particular claims in mind (for example `bs:C3`, `bs:C4` or `bs:C5`), please name them.
- Please also say what the concern is about: the theory, the evidence, how the institutional account is represented, or how strongly the conclusions are worded.
- It is just as useful to know what you consider settled, so the reviewer does not spend effort there.

**bs:E4. Journal standards and process.** Is there anything about the journal's standards or this review that the reviewer should weigh? For example:
- the round: a first submission or a revision (if a revision, the earlier reports and the response letter);
- the intended readership: a generalist organization-science audience, or a specialist strategy, information-systems or health-services one;
- the journal's policy on code and data, and whether the reviewer may run checks on supplied materials;
- the recommendation categories, the report format and the deadline.

**How your answers will be used.** I will summarize them as `bs:EB`, which records what you need, your concerns and the audience. Please correct it if I have misread you. The brief tells the reviewer what you need. It does not set their standards for them.

**Draft `bs:EB`, from the invitation alone** (your answers will replace it):
- **needs:** a reading of the transaction-cost model and of the empirical design (`inv:note`).
- **concerns:** the strength of the claims against the institutional account (`inv:note`). You have not yet said which claims, or on what grounds.
- **audience:** not stated.

---

**Notes for the workbench** (these are not part of the message to the editor)
- The message stays within the Mode E limit: four questions, in one message. The lists under each question are options to choose from, not extra questions.
- Everything above comes only from the invitation. I made no claims about the manuscript's substance. `bs:C1`–`bs:C5` are what the abstract says, quoted with their sentence locus. They are not findings.
- When the answers come in, my ranking of `bs:C1`–`bs:C5` and the answers to `bs:E2` and `bs:E3` will set the order of Round 2 in Mode S.
- **Uncertainty:** I am assuming `inv:note` is the whole of the editor's note.

**Decisions for the reviewer**
- There is nothing to decide yet: Mode E is an exchange between the elicitor and the editor.
- Once the editor answers, you will see `bs:EB` before Mode S begins. You can then say whether it matches your own reading of the invitation.

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_02_editor.md`

**Handling editor: answers to `bs:E0`**

Thanks. My answers are short and take precedence over my note.

**bs:E1. Main contribution.**
The paper's main selling point is C3, as the title shows. C4 makes the same claim more broadly, so merge the two. Below is how I rank what matters, and the order I'd like the review to follow:
1. **C1, together with its link to C2.** The modularity mechanism is the most interesting thing in the paper and is what would make it publishable. But I'm not confident the model and the empirics connect (see E3). So treat C1 and C2 as one question: does the model predict what is tested, and does the test find it?
2. **C3/C4, merged.** This is the headline, and it's the claim I'm least sure the evidence supports.
3. **C2 on its own.** The panel is unusually long: 412 hospitals over 11 years, balanced. The regularity has value even if the theory and the adjudication need work.
4. **C5.** Low priority. Flag it if you know of an earlier study that does this; don't search the literature for one.

**bs:E2. Why this reviewer.**
I chose them for transaction-cost theory and panel econometrics. I've invited a second reviewer to cover institutional theory, so this reviewer doesn't need to defend or critique that theory on its own terms. They do need to judge whether the empirical test of the rival (H3) is a fair one, because that's a question of design.
How deep:
- **Model:** re-derive it. The model is about a page (§2.2–2.3) and the proofs are short (Appendix). Checking that both propositions, including the uncertainty interaction, follow from the stated assumptions is cheap, and I want it done.
- **Empirics:** a reasoned reading of the identification (fixed effects, the controls, the event study described in the robustness paragraph), plus spot checks of the numbers in Table 2 and the text. I haven't seen any code or data with the submission, so no re-running.
- **Hospital IT setting:** nobody is specifically covering it. Flag anything obvious, but don't go looking.

**bs:E3. My concerns.**
I have two, both from one quick read.
1. **Do the model and the empirics actually connect? (C1 and C2.)** The model gives an outsourcing threshold for individual functions, but the outcome measured is a share of spending. The uncertainty result also goes the wrong way. H2 predicts a stronger modularity effect when uncertainty is high. Table 2 (Model 3) shows a negative interaction, which the authors call "contrary to H2", and §5 explains it with something outside the model. I want to know whether that's a failed prediction, a problem in the model or a problem in the test. This concern is about the theory and the evidence together.
2. **Is the dismissal of the institutional account fair? (C3, C4, and the "rule out" wording in the abstract and §5.)** Part of this is about how the rival is represented. Mimicry is tested with a single measure: the lagged mean outsourcing of other sample hospitals in the same state (§3.2). Part is about evidence. A peer coefficient that loses significance once modularity is added is not obviously enough to rule anything out. And part is about wording. It also sits oddly that §5 explains the H2 result with legitimacy pressures, an institutional mechanism, in a paper that claims to have ruled that account out. The second reviewer will speak to institutional theory. From this reviewer I want the evidence side.

Settled, so don't spend effort there: the question matters, and the mechanism deserves to be taken seriously. A long, balanced panel is a real asset, though the authors acknowledge in §5.2 that requiring a response in every year may skew the sample. C5 needs little effort (see E1).

**bs:E4. Journal and process.**
- This is the first round on an original submission, so there are no earlier reports or response letter.
- The readership is broad: this is a generalist organization-science journal. The paper has to speak to both the economics and the sociology of organizations. I'd like the reviewer to say whether a sociologist would find the model and the claims clear and fair, not only whether an economist would find them correct.
- Code and data: none came with the manuscript as I have it, so the reviewer should give a reasoned reading with spot checks only.
- Recommendation categories, format and deadline: nothing to add beyond the invitation.

**Corrections to the draft `bs:EB`.**
- **needs:** re-derive the model (both propositions); give a reasoned reading of the identification, with spot checks of the reported numbers; judge whether H3 is a fair test of the rival.
- **concerns:** (1) the link between model and empirics, including the H2 result; (2) the fairness and wording of the case against the institutional account (C3/C4).
- **audience:** generalist organization-science readers, both economists and sociologists of organizations. First round.

— Handling editor

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_02_editor_standin_note.md`

*Out-of-role note returned by the editor stand-in to the orchestrating session, alongside turn 2. It was not shown to the elicitor or the reviewer. Recorded verbatim because it bears on how the demonstration should be read (appendix §4.0).*

Notes on how I played the role:
- **Kept to what the editor knows.** The role says the editor read the manuscript once, quickly, and leaves the deeper checks to the reviewer, so the answer only voices those concerns. Checking it myself, I found that the proof of Proposition 2 leaves out the H'(u) term. Done correctly, Assumption A3 makes the cross-partial negative, which would match the negative interaction in Table 2. The editor's answer does not say this, so the reviewer still has to find it, though it does ask for the model to be re-derived.
- **Left unknowns unfilled.** The role file says nothing about the journal's code and data policy, its recommendation categories or the deadline. The editor says "nothing to add" on these rather than making them up.

##### (b) Mode S, Round 1 (recall): questions to the reviewer (`bs:S1`)

Dear Reviewer,

**The editor brief in short.** The full brief (`bs:EB`) is above. The editor chose you for transaction-cost theory and panel econometrics, and would like you to do four things:
- re-derive the model;
- give a reasoned reading of the identification, with spot checks of the reported numbers (no code or data were supplied);
- judge whether the empirical test of the institutional rival (H3) is a fair one;
- say whether a sociologist of organizations would find the model and the claims clear and fair.

A second reviewer covers institutional theory. If anything in `bs:EB` does not match your reading of the invitation, please say so.

**Before we draft your standards, four recall questions.**
- **Answer from past reviews, not this manuscript.** The aim is to record the standards you hold at your best before you read this paper, so that they are not fitted to it. If you have already read the manuscript, please tell me, and I will keep your reactions to it separate.
- **A few sentences each is enough.**
- **Do not identify any paper, author or journal.** You may paste anonymized excerpts from past reports if that is easier.

**bs:S1.1. Your proudest review.** Which review are you proudest of, and what made it good? You might mention what you checked, what you caught, how you put it to the authors, and what came of it.

**bs:S1.2. A rejection.** Think of a paper you recommended rejecting. What was the decisive reason, the one whose repair would have changed your recommendation?

**bs:S1.3. Checks you skip under time pressure.** Which checks do you perform "on a good day" but skip when time is short? Some examples:
- re-deriving a proof;
- recomputing a statistic from the reported coefficients and standard errors;
- reading the appendix;
- checking that each measure matches its construct;
- checking a priority claim.

**bs:S1.4. Your home tradition.** What is your home tradition? Which of its commitments should a paper be challenged on, rather than allowed to take for granted, including when the paper is written from within that tradition? Please answer in your own words. If an entry in the workbench catalogue of material inferences (MI1–MI10) captures what you mean, name it, and say whether you endorse it, reject it, or think it must be argued for each time.

**What happens next.** In Round 2 I will draft:
- a candidate setting for each of the five dimensions;
- 10 to 16 candidate standards, each tied to the words of yours that suggested it;
- for each dimension, at most two further standards of my own, clearly marked as my suggestions.

You will accept, reject or rewrite each one and set the five weights. The order will follow `bs:EB.elicitation_order`.

**Decisions for the reviewer**
- Does `bs:EB` match your reading of the invitation? Correct it if not.
- If you have already read the manuscript, say so, so that your reactions to it are kept apart from your recalled standards.
- Optionally, share anonymized excerpts from past reports. I will use them to propose standards in Round 2.

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_04_reviewer_S1.md`

**Focal reviewer: reply to Mode S, Round 1 (`bs:S1`)** (Reviewership v0.1)

##### Where I stand

I have not read the manuscript. I have the title, abstract and editor's note from the invitation, and now your brief. The brief itself tells me several things about the paper: the sign of the Model 3 interaction, how the peer measure is built, what §5 says about legitimacy, and that the outcome is a spending share. I can't unread those. My answers below come from past reviews, but I gave them after seeing the editor's concerns, so please don't fit my standards to those specifics. I've kept the few reactions I already have to this paper in a separate section at the end.

##### On `bs:EB`

It broadly matches. I have five notes.

1. **Scope.** The invitation asked for two things: a reading of the transaction-cost model and a reading of the empirical design, given the paper's strong claims against the institutional account. The brief asks for more (N4 to N6, and the depth settings), on the strength of editor answers I haven't seen. I accept these on the editor's authority.
2. **N4.** I can judge whether a non-economist could follow the model as stated, and whether the paper describes the rival in terms its own proponents would recognise. On the first I'm a competent reader. On the second I'm not an expert, so if the second reviewer disagrees with me, defer to them.
3. **N3 and the division of labour.** To judge whether the test of H3 is fair, I need a view of what mimetic isomorphism predicts. I'll take the rival's prediction as the institutional literature usually states it. Then I'll judge the design against that prediction: does the measure capture the construct, and can the test tell the two accounts apart? The content of institutional theory belongs to the second reviewer.
4. **Ranking.** `bs:C2` appears at rank 1 (merged with C1) and again at rank 3 (alone). I read rank 1 as "does the model connect to the test" and rank 3 as "the panel regularity as a finding in its own right". If that's what you mean, fine. If not, please fix it.
5. **Settled items.** I accept that the editor wants no effort spent on the balanced-panel restriction as a question of representativeness. But requiring a response in every year also selects on survival. Closures and mergers in this period may be correlated with both the regressor and the outcome. If that bears on identification, I'll say so in one sentence and no more.

**Depth.** Re-deriving the model and spot-checking the numbers are my good-day checks (see S1.3). The editor has asked for both, and a one-page model with short proofs fits in a sitting, so I'll do them. If the hour runs out, I'll cut from the bottom of the editor's list (N6, then N5, then N4), never from N1 to N3.

##### bs:S1.1 Proudest review

**The paper.** A firm panel on a governance choice and its performance consequences. It used firm fixed effects, and firms adopted the treatment at different times. The headline coefficient was large and survived every specification the authors tried.

**What I caught.** I asked where the identifying variation came from. With firm fixed effects, it came only from the firms that switched, a minority. The descriptives suggested those firms had been doing badly just before they switched. That is an Ashenfelter dip: part of the post-switch "effect" was recovery towards the mean.

**How I put it to the authors.** I didn't assert it. I said I might be wrong and explained what I thought was happening. I asked for an event-study plot with leads and a comparison against firms that had not yet switched. I also said in advance what pattern would persuade me the effect was real.

**What came of it.** The leads were negative and significant. Once the dip was handled, the effect was about half its original size but still there. The paper was better for it, and the authors thanked me in their response letter.

**What made it good:**
- I went to the source of the variation, not down the list of robustness checks.
- I proposed a test whose result I didn't know.
- I said beforehand what would change my mind.
- I framed it as a problem to solve, not a gotcha.

##### bs:S1.2 A rejection

**The paper.** A transaction-cost paper with a verbal model and three hypotheses. The main-effect hypothesis followed from the argument. The two moderation hypotheses did not. The argument said nothing about how the moderators interact with specificity. The signs the authors chose rested on an assumption they never stated, and under the opposite assumption, which was equally plausible, the signs reversed. The empirics were competent.

**The decisive reason.** A hypothesis that does not follow from the theory cannot test it. Support for it doesn't confirm the theory, and its failure doesn't damage the theory.

**The repair that would have changed my recommendation** (to major revision): either state the assumption that signs the interactions and defend it, ideally by formalising it, or drop the theory claim for those hypotheses and present them as exploratory.

**Two views I took from that case:**
- A prediction that follows from the theory and fails is a result, not a reason to reject. I'd want it reported as such, with the consequence for the theory drawn out.
- A failed prediction rescued after the fact by a mechanism the theory doesn't contain is a cost to the theory, not a save.

I know the second view sits close to one of the editor's concerns here. I've held it for a long time; it is not a verdict on this paper.

##### bs:S1.3 Checks I skip under time pressure

**What I skip,** roughly in the order I let them go:
- **Priority claims.** I almost never check these. I flag an earlier paper only if I happen to know one.
- **The appendix.** I read it only if the main text sends me there or something looks off.
- **Recomputing statistics.** For example: t from b/se; stars against t; whether N is consistent across tables and with the sample description; whether a reported interaction gives the marginal effects the text claims across the range of the moderator; whether magnitudes are economically plausible given the descriptives.
- **Re-deriving proofs.** Under pressure I check only that each proposition's sign makes intuitive sense and that the comparative statics go the stated way. I don't check that the proof works.
- **Measure–construct fit for controls.** I still check it for the main regressor and the outcome, because a bad measure there is an identification problem. I stop checking it for the controls.

**What I never skip:** where the identifying variation comes from; the fixed-effects structure and what it absorbs; reverse causality and the obvious omitted variables; whether the comparison group makes sense.

**My honest worry about myself.** The checks I skip are the ones that catch an internally inconsistent paper. The identification check catches a confounded one. When I'm rushed, I miss more of the first kind.

##### bs:S1.4 Home tradition

My tradition is Williamsonian transaction-cost economics, with a panel-econometrics habit. These are the commitments a paper should have to argue for, including a paper written from inside TCE.

1. **Asset specificity as exogenous.** Firms often choose specificity together with governance: a firm that plans to outsource designs for it. Regressing governance on specificity assumes a direction of causation, and the paper must either argue for it or identify it.
2. **Discriminating alignment as an equilibrium.** The claim that observed governance is economizing rests on selection weeding out misaligned forms. That needs competition and time. Where selection pressure is weak, as with nonprofits or regulated sectors, it can't be assumed and must be argued each time.
3. **The sign of the uncertainty interaction.** In Williamson, uncertainty matters through specificity. But the sign of any interaction depends on what uncertainty does in the model. If it raises the cost of adapting through the market, it favours internal governance. If it raises the value of flexibility, it can favour buying. Either way, the sign has to be derived, not asserted.
4. **Economizing as the default explanation.** TCE stories are easy to tell after the fact, especially when specificity is measured loosely or inferred from the outcome. Consistency with economizing counts as evidence for it only where the rival predicts something different.
   - I hold my own tradition to the same falsifiability standard I apply to institutional accounts.
   - I'm inclined to find institutional accounts hard to falsify. That's a bias of mine, and you should hold me to it.
5. **Rivals as mutually exclusive.** Economizing and institutional mechanisms can operate together.
   - To rule out a rival, you need a test on which the two accounts predict different things, with the rival measured in a way its proponents would accept.
   - A coefficient that loses significance when a correlated regressor is added is not that test. The loss can reflect collinearity, differential measurement error (the better-measured variable wins), or mediation.
   - I've made this point in past reviews.

**On MI1 to MI10.** I haven't been shown the catalogue, so I can't name entries. Map these points onto it yourself and show me each entry's wording in Round 2. I'll endorse it, reject it, or say it must be argued for each time. The same goes for the parameter codes (TEC.2, INF.3 and so on): I'll respond to their wording, not the codes.

##### Excerpt from a past report (anonymized)

From the S1.1 review:

> "I may be wrong about this, but as I read the main table the fixed-effects estimate is identified only from the firms that switch, and the descriptives suggest they switch after a bad patch. Could you show the outcome in event time, with leads, against firms that have not yet switched? If the leads are flat, I'd be persuaded the effect is real."

##### Reactions to this paper so far (keep separate from my standards)

These come from the abstract and the brief only, and I haven't checked them.

- **(a)** The abstract presents the uncertainty interaction as a prediction of the model, but it doesn't report the result the editor describes. If the editor is right about the sign, the abstract should say so.
- **(b)** "Rule out" and "first study to adjudicate directly" are strong claims. I'll read the paper to see whether the design supports them.

Some traditions accept these inferences without argument, and others challenge them. For each one, choose:
- **endorse:** you accept it without argument;
- **reject:** you do not accept it;
- **argue each time:** a paper must argue for it whenever it relies on it;
- **neutral:** no view.

##### 4. Draft standards (16)

For each standard, please say **accept**, **reject** or **rewrite** (and give your wording). Each has a proposed priority: must, should or could. In Round 3, I will make each standard checkable and point out any that pull against each other.

###### Inferential

`std:1` **Hypotheses that test a theory must be derived from it.**
- **Standard.** A hypothesis offered as a test of the theory must follow from the theory's stated assumptions. For an interaction, the paper states and defends the assumption that fixes its sign. A hypothesis that does not follow is labelled exploratory, and it counts neither for nor against the theory.
- **Your words.** "A hypothesis that does not follow from the theory cannot test it." (`rv:S1.2`); "the sign has to be derived, not asserted" (`rv:S1.4.3`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must, because it was your decisive reason in `rv:S1.2`.

`std:2` **Failed predictions are results; after-the-fact rescues are costs.**
- **Standard.** A prediction that follows from the theory and fails is reported as a result, and its consequence for the theory is drawn out. An explanation added afterwards, using a mechanism the theory does not contain, is labelled as such and counted against the theory, not for it.
- **Your words.** Both of the views you drew from the case in `rv:S1.2`. You noted that this sits close to one of the editor's concerns. I have recorded it as your long-held view, not as a verdict on this paper.
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:3` **Ruling out a rival needs a discriminating test.**
- **Standard.** To claim that a rival account is ruled out, the paper needs a test on which the two accounts predict different things, with the rival's key construct measured in a way its proponents would accept. Evidence consistent with the paper's own account supports it only where the rival predicts something different.
- **Your words.** "To rule out a rival, you need a test on which the two accounts predict different things" (`rv:S1.4.5`); "Consistency with economizing counts as evidence for it only where the rival predicts something different" (`rv:S1.4.4`); `rv:EB.3`.
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:4` **A lost significance star is not a null result.**
- **Standard.** A coefficient that loses significance when a correlated regressor is added is not evidence that the variable has no effect. Before drawing that conclusion, the paper addresses collinearity, differential measurement error and mediation.
- **Your words.** "The loss can reflect collinearity, differential measurement error (the better-measured variable wins), or mediation" (`rv:S1.4.5`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

###### Technical

`std:5` **Re-derive the model.**
- **Standard.** When a formal model is supplied, re-derive each proposition from the stated assumptions, including the sign of any interaction. Checking that the signs look intuitive is not enough.
- **Your words.** "Under pressure I check only that each proposition's sign makes intuitive sense ... I don't check that the proof works" (`rv:S1.3`); `rv:depth`.
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:6` **Spot-check the numbers.** Check:
- t against b/se;
- the significance stars against t;
- N across tables, and against the sample description;
- whether a reported interaction gives the marginal effects the text claims, across the range of the moderator;
- whether the magnitudes are economically plausible given the descriptive statistics.

**Your words.** The recomputation list in `rv:S1.3`. **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

###### Ontological

`std:7` **Measures fit their constructs for the main variables.**
- **Standard.** The fit between measure and construct is argued, not assumed, for the main regressor and the outcome. An attribute that bears on governance, such as asset specificity, is not inferred from the outcome it is meant to explain.
- **Your words.** "a bad measure there is an identification problem" (`rv:S1.3`); "especially when specificity is measured loosely or inferred from the outcome" (`rv:S1.4.4`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must. Should this extend to controls? See ONT.4.

`std:8` **Economizing claims must show selection.**
- **Standard.** A claim that observed governance is economizing (that is, efficient, or an optimal response) must show, or argue for, the selection pressure that would weed out misaligned forms: competition and time. Where selection is weak, as in nonprofit or regulated sectors, it cannot be assumed.
- **Your words.** "Where selection pressure is weak, as with nonprofits or regulated sectors, it can't be assumed and must be argued each time" (`rv:S1.4.2`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** should.

`std:9` **[suggestion] Unit of theory and unit of test.**
- **Standard.** If the theory predicts at one level and the test is run at another, the paper shows how the prediction carries over to the tested level. That includes the sign of any interaction on the scale on which it is tested. (In transaction-cost economics, for example, the theory is about individual transactions, but tests are often run on organization-level aggregates.)
- **Why a demanding reviewer in your field would hold it.** Williamson takes the transaction as the basic unit of analysis (Williamson 1985, to verify), so a firm-level test needs an aggregation step.
- **Disclosure.** This bears on the editor's concern `bs:EB.K1`.
- **Proposed priority:** should.

###### Epistemological

`std:10` **Find the source of the identifying variation.**
- **Standard.** The paper shows four things: what the fixed effects absorb; which units supply the variation; whether those units differed from the others before treatment; and that the comparison group makes sense. Where units adopt at different times, it shows estimates in event time, with leads, against units not yet treated.
- **Your words.** "I went to the source of the variation, not down the list of robustness checks" (`rv:S1.1`); "an event-study plot with leads and a comparison against firms that had not yet switched" (`rv:S1.1`); your list of what you never skip (`rv:S1.3`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:11` **Direction of causation for attributes chosen together with governance.**
- **Standard.** Where governance is regressed on an attribute that firms may choose together with governance (asset specificity is the standard case), the paper argues for or identifies the direction of causation. Reverse causality and the obvious omitted variables are addressed.
- **Your words.** "Regressing governance on specificity assumes a direction of causation, and the paper must either argue for it or identify it" (`rv:S1.4.1`); your list of what you never skip (`rv:S1.3`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:12` **Symmetry.**
- **Standard.** The review holds the paper's own transaction-cost account to the same falsifiability standard as the rival. Economizing is not treated as the default explanation. The reviewer checks the draft for a tendency to find institutional accounts hard to falsify.
- **Your words.** "I hold my own tradition to the same falsifiability standard I apply to institutional accounts"; "That's a bias of mine, and you should hold me to it" (`rv:S1.4.4`).
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must. This standard applies to your review, not to the paper. Mode C will check it.

`std:13` **[suggestion] Claims of absence need bounds.**
- **Standard.** To conclude that a variable has no effect, the paper reports the estimate with its confidence interval and shows that effects large enough to matter are excluded. One way is an equivalence test against a stated smallest effect of interest.
- **Why.** `std:4` says what does not show a null result. This standard says what would.
- **Disclosure.** This bears on the evidence side of the editor's concern `bs:EB.K2`.
- **Proposed priority:** should.

`std:14` **[suggestion] Peer influence versus shared conditions.**
- **Standard.** A measure of peers' earlier adoption counts as evidence of imitation only if the design separates imitation from peers responding in the same way to shared conditions, such as common shocks or common regulation.
- **Why.** This is the standard identification problem for peer effects (Manski 1993, the "reflection problem", to verify).
- **Disclosure.** This bears on `bs:EB.N3` and on a detail the brief reports. Reject it if it reads as fitted.
- **Proposed priority:** should.

###### Pragmatic

`std:15` **Problems to solve, not gotchas.**
- **Standard.** The reviewer:
  - says where they may be wrong;
  - proposes a test whose result they do not know;
  - says in advance what result would change their mind;
  - names the repair that would change the recommendation;
  - keeps decisive problems apart from fixable ones. This last point is my addition, drawn from how `rv:S1.2` separates "the decisive reason" from "the repair".
- **Your words.** The four bullets under "What made it good" (`rv:S1.1`); your excerpt: "If the leads are flat, I'd be persuaded the effect is real."
- **Origin:** reviewer. **Proposed priority:** must.

`std:16` **Readable by non-economists; rival recognisable.**
- **Standard.** The model's assumptions, and what drives each prediction, are stated so that a reader without economics training can follow them. The rival is described in terms its proponents would recognise. On this second point, you defer to the second reviewer.
- **Your words.** "I can judge whether a non-economist could follow the model as stated" (`rv:EB.2`).
- **Origin:** reviewer (from the editor's need N4). **Proposed priority:** should, because it is the third thing you would cut under time pressure (`bs:EB.ann6`).

###### In reserve

These are further suggestions of mine and are not among the 16. If you want one, swap it for a standard you reject, so the list stays at 16 or fewer.
- **TEC:** standard errors are clustered at the level at which the key regressors vary.
- **TEC:** for a revision, ask for code and data sufficient to reproduce the main tables.
- **PRA:** the abstract and conclusions report results that go against the hypotheses, and state conclusions no more strongly than the design supports. Disclosure: this overlaps with your reactions `bs:RX.a` and `bs:RX.b`, which I have otherwise kept apart.

##### 5. How to reply

Short answers are fine. For example: "std:8 accept, must · std:13 rewrite: … · MI3 neutral · TEC.5 simulation OK if verified · weights INF 0.8 …". I will treat anything you don't mention as unanswered, not as accepted.

**Decisions for the reviewer**
- Accept, reject or rewrite each of `std:1` to `std:16`, and confirm or change its priority.
- Choose a stance on each of the inferences MI1 to MI10.
- Fill in the open settings. "No view" counts as an answer. The open settings are:
  - INF.5; INF.6 (assimilative and reductive);
  - TEC.1; TEC.5;
  - ONT.2; ONT.4 (controls); ONT.5 (functional and constitutive);
  - EPI.1; EPI.3 (model-based); EPI.5 (pre-registration); EPI.6 (informants);
  - PRA.2; PRA.4.
- Set the five weights.
- Say whether any reserve standard should replace one of the 16.

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_06_reviewer_S2.md`

**Focal reviewer: reply to Mode S, Round 2 (`bs:S2`)** (Reviewership v0.1)

I still have not read the manuscript. My answers follow your order.

##### A general note first

All three of your suggestions bear on the editor's concerns, and so does one reserve standard. I've accepted the ones I would hold for any paper, and I say so at each. But the result is a standard set aimed mostly at finding faults that the editor already suspects. To balance it, I've added "say what survives" to `std:15`, and I've widened `std:12` to cover both halves of my bias. Mode C should check both.

##### 1. Annotations on the brief

- **ann1:** Accept. Yes, please pass on the editor's own words for E1 to E4 before I draft. I'd rather read the editor than a summary. I don't need them for the standards.
- **ann2, ann3, ann5, ann6:** Accept. That includes the Mode C check on the one sentence about survival selection.
- **ann4:** Thanks.

##### 2. Settings

###### INF

- **INF.1:** Accept. Inference to the best explanation between rivals needs discriminating evidence (`std:3`).
- **INF.3, INF.4, INF.7:** Accept.
- **INF.5:** Depth, meaning a mechanism specified closely enough to yield an implication the data could refute. Coverage is welcome. But a mechanism that covers everything predicts nothing.
- **INF.6:**
  - *Eliminative:* accept as proposed.
  - *Assimilative:* argue each time. Reinterpreting the rival's evidence as ours counts only if the reinterpretation yields a prediction the original reading doesn't. Otherwise it is relabelling.
  - *Reductive:* accepted when the paper shows that the lower-level mechanism produces the pattern, not merely that it is consistent with it. I have no view on reductionism as such.

###### TEC

- **TEC.1:** Preferred, not required at first round. For a revision, I ask for code that reproduces the main tables, plus the data where the licence allows. This covers the code-and-data reserve standard, so it needn't be a standard.
- **TEC.2:** Accept. "Recompute" means spot checks, not every cell.
- **TEC.3:** Accept, with two additions:
  - with staggered adoption, an estimator robust to effects that differ across adoption cohorts (see `std:10`);
  - clustering (see the new `std:9`).
- **TEC.4:** Accept.
- **TEC.5:** A closed form is preferred, not required. A simulation is acceptable if the parameter ranges are reported and the claimed comparative statics hold across them, not at one chosen point. For a one-page model, I expect a closed form.

###### ONT

- **ONT.1:** Accept, with one change. The actors are boundedly rational *and* capable of opportunism, since both are Williamson's behavioural assumptions. Institutional entities are admissible if they are specified so as to yield a prediction. No view on others.
- **ONT.2:** Cross-level allowed, with an explicit bridge. I've built this into `std:1` (see `std:9` below).
- **ONT.3:** Accept.
- **ONT.4:** Strict for the main regressor, the outcome and the rival's key construct. Moderate for controls, except strict for any control that carries identifying weight: one whose inclusion moves a key coefficient, or that stands in for a rival's construct.
- **ONT.5:** Accept for causal, choice-theoretic and selection explanations.
  - *Functional:* rejected unless a selection or feedback mechanism is shown. "It exists because it serves a function" is not an explanation by itself.
  - *Constitutive:* no view; outside my competence.

###### EPI

- **EPI.1:** Realist. Mechanisms are real and are tested through their observable implications. I don't accept the "as if" defence for the assumption that does the work in a model.
- **EPI.2:** I accept the label, read as Lakatos rather than naive Popper (see my rewrite of `std:2`).
- **EPI.3:** Design-based preferred. Model-based assumptions are acceptable if they are stated, argued, and tested where they can be (placebos, overidentification). They are not a substitute where a design-based route is available.
- **EPI.4:** Accept.
- **EPI.5:** Accept. Pre-registration is not expected for archival panel work, and I don't penalise its absence. I do expect the paper to say how the main specification was chosen and to report the ones that didn't work.
- **EPI.6:** Accept. On informants: a single informant is fine for factual items such as spending. For perceptual constructs, I expect multiple informants or a validation.

###### PRA

- **PRA.1, PRA.3, PRA.5, PRA.6:** Accept.
- **PRA.2:** In my order of preference:
  1. A derived implication, credibly tested.
  2. Questioning an assumption the field holds.
  3. Gap-filling alone, which counts least.

  Being "interesting" in Davis's sense is welcome but not sufficient. A paper that denies what its audience takes for granted carries a higher burden of evidence. Your citation is right as I remember it: Davis (1971), "That's Interesting!", *Philosophy of the Social Sciences*.
- **PRA.4:** No view. Implications for practice are not a criterion for me, unless the paper makes claims about practice. Then those claims must follow from the evidence.

##### 3. Weights

| Dimension | Weight | Why |
|---|---|---|
| INF | 0.9 | My decisive rejection was an inference failure. |
| EPI | 0.9 | Identification is the one thing I never skip. |
| TEC | 0.7 | High at my best. A numerical slip is usually fixable unless it signals something deeper. |
| ONT | 0.6 | Matters most where measurement is itself an identification problem. |
| PRA | 0.4 | Governs how I write more than what I conclude. Over-claiming I treat under INF and EPI. |

##### 4. Field-specific inferences (MI1 to MI10)

| Id | Stance | Note |
|---|---|---|
| MI1 | Endorse as theory, with your empirical proviso (`std:11`) | One caveat: in-house is one safeguard among several. Long-term contracts and hostages are others. |
| MI2 | Argue each time | Accept. |
| MI3 | Argue each time | Accept. The reverse also holds: spread among peers is not evidence *against* imitation just because an economizing variable also predicts it. |
| MI4 | Argue each time, for the step from adoption to use | Decoupling is real. A paper that measures adoption and theorises about use must argue the link. |
| MI5 | Neutral | Not my area. |
| MI6 | Endorse only as a conditional | Accept. With staggered timing, the estimator must also be robust to heterogeneous effects. |
| MI7 | Reject | Accept. |
| MI8 | Argue each time | It's an empirical claim about a technology, not a theoretical premise. Standard interfaces can relocate specificity rather than remove it, for example into lock-in to a vendor or platform. The direction can also run the other way: firms that plan to outsource adopt standards (`std:11`). I find it plausible, which is why I want it argued. |
| MI9 | Argue each time | Accept. Where there are multiple equilibria, "equilibrium" does not mean "optimal". |
| MI10 | Neutral | The second reviewer's domain. I don't reject it: a legitimacy argument that predicts something an efficiency argument doesn't is testable, and I'll treat it so. |

##### 5. Standards

###### `std:1` Hypotheses must be derived from the theory

**Rewrite, must.** I've folded `std:9` in:

> A hypothesis offered as a test of the theory must follow from the theory's stated assumptions, at the level and on the scale at which it is tested. Where the theory is about transactions and the test is about organizations, the paper states the aggregation step. It also shows that each predicted sign, including the sign of any interaction, survives that step. For an interaction, the paper states and defends the assumption that fixes its sign. A hypothesis that does not follow is labelled exploratory, and it counts neither for nor against the theory.

###### `std:2` Failed predictions and after-the-fact rescues

**Rewrite, must.**

> A prediction that follows from the theory and fails is reported as a result wherever the prediction is stated, including the abstract and the conclusions, and its consequence for the theory is drawn out. An explanation added afterwards, using a mechanism the theory does not contain, is labelled as such and does not count as support. It counts against the theory unless the mechanism is built into the model and yields a further prediction that the data could reject and do not.

The words "including the abstract and the conclusions" come from your reserve PRA standard, which I hold in general. Record that they overlap my reaction `bs:RX.a`.

###### `std:3` Ruling out a rival needs a discriminating test

**Rewrite, must.** I've added two sentences at the end:

> The rival's prediction is taken as its own literature usually states it. Without a discriminating test, the paper may say that its evidence does not require the rival, not that the rival is ruled out, and it states its conclusions no more strongly than the design supports.

The last clause also comes from the reserve standard. Record that it overlaps `bs:RX.b`.

###### `std:4` A lost significance star is not a null result

**Accept, must.**

###### `std:5` Re-derive the model

**Rewrite, must.** Add at the end:

> and check that each proof uses only assumptions stated in the set-up.

This is exactly what I skip under pressure. Mode C should check that I did it.

###### `std:6` Spot-check the numbers

**Rewrite, must.** Add a bullet:

> the text describes each result as the table shows it: its sign, its significance, and which model it comes from.

###### `std:7` Measures fit their constructs

**Rewrite, must.** Extend it to controls as set in ONT.4:

> …and for any control that carries identifying weight.

###### `std:8` Economizing claims must show selection

**Rewrite.** Priority: should, and must where efficiency is the paper's conclusion.

> A claim that a governance choice is efficient, meaning an optimal response and not merely a choice that responds to transaction attributes as the theory predicts, must show or argue for the selection pressure that would weed out misaligned forms: competition and time. Where selection is weak, as in nonprofit or regulated sectors, it cannot be assumed. A claim only about motive (that choices track transaction attributes) does not need this.

###### `std:9` Unit of theory and unit of test [suggestion]

**Accept the substance, folded into `std:1`.** It is `std:1` applied to aggregation. I should have listed it myself, since the transaction is Williamson's unit of analysis. Your citation (Williamson 1985) is right as I remember it.

Use the freed slot for the clustering reserve, which I accept as **must**:

> Standard errors are clustered at the level at which the key regressors vary, or the paper explains why not. With few clusters, a small-cluster correction is used.

I check this whenever I check identification. I left it off my Round 1 list by oversight.

###### `std:10` Find the source of the identifying variation

**Rewrite, must.** Replace the last sentence with:

> Where a discrete treatment is adopted at different times, it shows estimates in event time, with leads, against units not yet treated, using an estimator robust to effects that differ across adoption cohorts. Where the treatment is continuous, it shows the analogous check: leads of the regressor, or pre-trends by later exposure.

###### `std:11` Direction of causation

**Accept, must.**

###### `std:12` Symmetry

**Rewrite, must.** Replace the last sentence with:

> The reviewer checks the draft for both halves of my bias: accepting an economizing account too readily, and dismissing an institutional account as unfalsifiable without asking whether the version at issue makes a testable prediction.

###### `std:13` Claims of absence need bounds [suggestion]

**Rewrite, should.** Keep it separate from `std:4`, so the record shows which half is mine.

> A claim that a variable has no effect reports the estimate and its confidence interval in the specification on which the claim rests, states in substantive terms the smallest effect that would matter, and shows that the interval excludes it. An equivalence test is one way to do this, not a requirement. Without such bounds, the paper may say only that the effect is not distinguishable from zero in this sample.

###### `std:14` Peer influence versus shared conditions [suggestion]

**Rewrite, should.** You chose this one because of the brief. But I'd apply it to any peer-effects paper, so I accept it, in a form that cuts both ways:

> A measure of peers' earlier adoption counts as evidence for *or against* imitation only if the design separates imitation from two things: peers responding alike to shared conditions (common shocks, common regulation, common suppliers), and selection into peer groups. Where the paper's own regressor may respond to the same shared conditions, the design addresses that too.

Your citation is right as I remember it: Manski (1993), the reflection problem, *Review of Economic Studies*.

###### `std:15` Problems to solve, not gotchas

**Rewrite, must.** I accept your addition about keeping decisive problems apart from fixable ones, and I add one more bullet:

> says what in the paper survives the criticisms, and what would be lost if it were not published.

###### `std:16` Readable by non-economists; rival recognisable

**Rewrite, should.**

> The model's assumptions, and what drives each prediction, are stated in words that a reader without economics training can follow, alongside the formal statement. The rival is described in terms its proponents would recognise; on this point I defer to the second reviewer.

##### 6. Reserve standards

- **Clustering:** In, in `std:9`'s slot.
- **Code and data:** Handled as the TEC.1 setting, not as a standard.
- **PRA (abstract and conclusions):** Folded into `std:2` and `std:3`, with the overlaps with `bs:RX.a` and `bs:RX.b` recorded.

The list stays at 16.

Dear Reviewer,

After your answers, I will write the specification. It is a specification of your standards, not a review.

##### 1. What I recorded from Round 2

Please correct anything I have recorded wrongly. I will treat silence as confirmation for this section only.

At minimum, a sketch that states every assumption fixing a sign; a formal derivation is preferred for interactions.<br>**Unstated premises:** low tolerance.<br>**What a good explanation does:** depth, meaning a mechanism specified closely enough to yield an implication the data could refute. Being "interesting" is welcome but not sufficient, and a paper that denies what its audience takes for granted carries a higher burden of evidence.<br>**Priority claims:** sometimes.<br>**Practice:** not a criterion, unless the paper makes claims about practice; then those claims must follow from the evidence.<br>**How the review is written:** `std:15`.<br>**Editor's needs:** `bs:EB` with your annotations. |

**Weights:** INF 0.9 · EPI 0.9 · TEC 0.7 · ONT 0.6 · PRA 0.4.

**Field-specific inferences (MI1–MI10):**
- **MI1** (hold-up and hierarchy): endorse as theory, with the empirical proviso in `std:11`. In-house governance is one safeguard among several; long-term contracts and hostages are others.

##### 2. The 16 standards in checkable form

For each standard I give three things:
- **Check (paper):** the conditions that must hold for the paper to pass.
- **Applied when:** what your draft must contain for Mode C to count the standard as applied.
- **Question:** where the standard needs a decision from you to become checkable. Each question has an id, `bs:Qn`.

The wording is yours. I have only split it into conditions, and anything I added is marked [mine]. For each standard, please confirm the checkable form or rewrite it.

---

**`std:1` Hypotheses must be derived from the theory, at the tested level and scale.** INF.3, ONT.2 · must · origin: reviewer (my suggestion, formerly `std:9`, is folded in)

**Check (paper).** Take each hypothesis the paper presents as a test of its theory. All of the following must hold:
- (a) It follows from a stated proposition, proof or explicit sketch.
- (b) Every assumption that fixes a predicted sign, including the sign of any interaction, is stated and defended.
- (c) If the theory's unit differs from the test's unit (for example, transactions versus organizations), the aggregation step is stated, and each predicted sign is shown to survive it on the scale of the variable actually tested.
- (d) Any hypothesis that fails (a)–(c) is labelled exploratory, and it is not counted for or against the theory.

**Applied when.** The draft takes each hypothesis in turn and gives a verdict on (a)–(c), citing where in the paper the support lies (proposition, proof or section). Where a hypothesis fails, the draft states what follows under (d) and what repair would fix it.

**Question.** See tension `bs:T1`.

---

**`std:2` Failed predictions are results; after-the-fact rescues are costs.** INF.1, EPI.2, EPI.4 · must · origin: reviewer (wording from my reserve standard folded in; overlaps `bs:RX.a`)

**Check (paper).** Take each derived prediction that fails in the reported tests.
- (a) The failure is reported as a failure everywhere the prediction is stated: the hypotheses, the results, the abstract and the conclusions.
- (b) The paper says what the failure implies for the theory, naming which assumption or step is now in doubt.
- (c) Any explanation offered afterwards, using a mechanism the model does not contain, is labelled as such and is not counted as support.
- (d) Such an explanation counts against the theory, unless the mechanism is built into the model and yields a further prediction that the data could reject and do not.

**Applied when.** For each failed prediction, the draft checks (a)–(d), citing where each is or is not met.

---

**`std:3` Ruling out a rival needs a discriminating test.** INF.7, INF.6 · must · origin: reviewer (wording from my reserve standard folded in; overlaps `bs:RX.b`)

**Check (paper).** Take each claim that a rival account is ruled out, or words to that effect.
- (a) The rival's prediction is stated as its own literature usually states it, with a citation.
- (b) At least one test is reported on which the two accounts predict different signs or patterns, and the paper says what each account predicts.
- (c) The rival's key construct is measured in a way its proponents would accept, and the paper argues this.
- (d) Evidence consistent with the paper's own account is counted as support only where the rival predicts something different.
- (e) If (b) or (c) fails, the paper says only that its evidence does not require the rival. Throughout, no conclusion is stated more strongly than the design supports.

**Applied when.** The draft locates each ruling-out claim, checks (a)–(e), and proposes weaker wording where (e) applies.

**Question.** Your judgement on (c) depends on the rival's content. See tension `bs:T2`.

---

**`std:4` A lost significance star is not a null result.** INF.2 (rejects MI7), EPI.5 · must · origin: reviewer

**Check (paper).** The paper may infer that a variable has no effect, or plays no role, from a coefficient that loses significance once a correlated regressor is added. Wherever it does, it addresses all three of the following:
- (a) collinearity between the two regressors (for example, their correlation, or a joint test) [the examples are mine];
- (b) differential measurement error, that is, which regressor is measured with more error;
- (c) mediation, that is, whether the added regressor lies on the causal path from the first.

The paper fails if any of the three is left unaddressed.

**Applied when.** The draft locates each such inference and names which of (a)–(c) the paper leaves unaddressed.

---

**`std:5` Re-derive the model.** TEC.2, TEC.5 · must · origin: reviewer · Mode C to check, at your request

**Check (by you).** For each proposition:
- (a) Re-derive it from the stated assumptions, including the sign of every comparative static and interaction it claims.
- (b) Check that each step of the proof uses only assumptions stated in the set-up, and list any unstated assumption that a step relies on.
- (c) [mine] Record the re-derivation as a check that the workbench harness can run, for example a `sympy` script for the signs of the derivatives and cross-partials. A finding about the model then reads "demonstrated" or "refuted-by-check", not "asserted".

**Applied when.** For each proposition, the draft says whether it follows and names any unstated assumption, with its location. If you accept (c), it also gives the id of the check and its result.

**Question `bs:Q1`.** Do you accept (c)? It is the workbench's rule for formal claims. You can do the re-derivation by hand and have the harness check it.

---

**`std:6` Spot-check the numbers.** TEC.4 · must · origin: reviewer

**Check (by you).** Check the following:
- (a) For the key coefficients, t is approximately b/se, allowing for rounding.
- (b) The significance stars match t (or p) under the stated thresholds.
- (c) N is consistent across tables and with the sample description.
- (d) For each reported interaction, the marginal effect of the focal variable across the observed range of the moderator matches what the text claims.
- (e) The magnitudes are economically plausible given the descriptive statistics, for example the implied change in the outcome for a one-standard-deviation change in the regressor.
- (f) The text describes each result as the table shows it: its sign, its significance, and which model it comes from.

**Applied when.** The draft lists which checks were run, on which cells, and with what result. If you accept `bs:Q1`, the computational checks are recorded as harness checks.

**Question `bs:Q2`.** What is the minimum spot check? My proposal: every coefficient on which a hypothesis test rests, every number quoted in the abstract, and every interaction for check (d). Do you accept this, or do you want to set your own minimum?

---

**`std:7` Measures fit their constructs.** ONT.4, EPI.6 · must · origin: reviewer

**Check (paper).** This standard covers the main regressor, the outcome, the rival's key construct, and any control that carries identifying weight. For each of these:
- (a) The construct is defined, and the paper argues that the measure captures it.
- (b) No governance-relevant attribute is measured by, or inferred from, the outcome it explains.
- (c) Perceptual constructs have multiple informants or a validation. Single-informant factual items are acceptable.

**Applied when.** The draft names each such variable and gives a verdict on (a)–(c), citing where in the paper each is addressed.

**Question `bs:Q3`.** A control "carries identifying weight" if its inclusion moves a key coefficient, or if it stands in for a rival's construct. To make this checkable, how much movement counts? My proposal: a change in sign, or a change in size that you state in advance as substantively meaningful. I have avoided a significance-based threshold because of `std:4`.

---

**`std:8` Efficiency claims must show selection.** ONT.3, INF.2 (MI2, MI9) · should, and must where efficiency is the paper's conclusion · origin: reviewer

**Check (paper).** Classify each of the paper's conclusions about governance as one of two kinds:
- (i) a claim about motive or alignment: choices track transaction attributes as the theory predicts;
- (ii) a claim about efficiency: the observed choice is an optimal response.

For each claim of kind (ii), the paper must show or argue for selection pressure, meaning competition and the time for selection to act. Where selection is weak, as in nonprofit or regulated sectors, it cannot be assumed. Claims of kind (i) do not need this.

**Applied when.** The draft classifies each governance conclusion, citing where it appears. For each kind-(ii) claim, it checks the argument for selection.

**Question `bs:Q4`.**
- **"Where efficiency is the conclusion":** my proposal is that this means stated in the abstract or the conclusions as what the results show. Do you accept that?

The word is common in transaction-cost work, and it appears in this invitation's abstract (sentence 7), so the answer matters here. I am asking for your general rule, not for a verdict on this paper.

- (d) that the comparison group makes sense;
- (e) for a discrete treatment adopted at different times: estimates in event time, with leads, against units not yet treated, using an estimator robust to effects that differ across adoption cohorts (for example Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021, or Sun and Abraham 2021; both to verify);

- (b) It states, in substantive terms, the smallest effect that would matter.
- (c) It shows that the interval excludes that effect. An equivalence test is one way to do this, but it is not required.
- (d) If it cannot do (a)–(c), it says only that the effect is not distinguishable from zero in this sample.

**`std:15` Problems to solve, not gotchas.** PRA.5 · must · origin: reviewer (with my clause on decisive versus fixable problems, accepted by you) · Mode C to check (f), at your request

- (c) says in advance what result would change your view;

**`std:16` Readable by non-economists; rival recognisable.** PRA.1 · should · origin: reviewer (from the editor's need N4)

**Check (paper).**
- (a) Each assumption of the model, and what drives each prediction, is stated in words alongside the formal statement. A reader without economics training could say, from the words alone, why each prediction has its sign.

**Applied when.** The draft gives a verdict on (a), naming any assumption or prediction that lacks a statement in words, and gives (b), marked as deferring.

##### 3. Tensions: please rank

Each tension below is a pair of your accepted standards that pull against each other. For each, please choose an option, or say which standard governs when the two conflict.

**`bs:T1`: `std:1` (derivation) versus `std:2` (failed predictions).**
- **The pull.** Under `std:1`, a hypothesis that does not follow from the theory counts neither for nor against it. Under `std:2`, a failed prediction counts against the theory. So the less carefully a hypothesis is derived, the less its failure costs the theory: `std:1` can shield a theory from `std:2`.
- **Option (a): `std:1` first.** A failed hypothesis that is not properly derived does not count against the theory. The paper's presentation of it as derived is a separate `std:1` failure, rated as a must on a dimension weighted 0.9. This respects the logical point that a prediction the theory does not entail cannot refute it.
- **Option (b): `std:2` governs where the paper presented the hypothesis as derived.** The failure counts against the theory as the paper states it, and `std:1` adds the derivation fault. This avoids rewarding under-derivation.
- **Option (c):** your own rule.

**`bs:T2`: Your judgements about the rival (`std:3` part c, `std:12` part c, `std:14`) versus your deferral on the rival's content (`std:16` part b, and the division of labour in `bs:EB`).**
- **The pull.** Three of your standards, two of them must, require judgements about institutional theory:
  - whether the rival's construct is measured in a way its proponents would accept (`std:3` c);
  - whether the version at issue makes a testable prediction (`std:12` c);
  - what imitation predicts, as opposed to shared conditions (`std:14`).
  But you defer to the second reviewer on the rival's content.
- **Option (a): judge provisionally.** Make each judgement, mark it as provisional, and defer if the second reviewer disagrees. This extends what you already do under `std:16` (b).
- **Option (b): split the work.** Keep your own verdicts to design and econometrics (`std:3` b and e, `std:14`). Put `std:3` (c) and `std:12` (c) to the editor as questions for the second reviewer, not as your verdicts.
- **Option (c):** your own rule.

**`bs:T3`: `std:10` (pre-trend checks) versus `std:13` and `std:4` (claims of absence).**
- **The pull.** A pre-trend check is itself a claim of absence: no difference before treatment. Your own past criterion was "If the leads are flat, I'd be persuaded". `std:4` and `std:13` say that non-significance alone does not establish absence. The ranking matters because `std:10` is must and `std:13` is should.
- **Option (a): `std:13` applies to leads.** The intervals on the leads must exclude pre-trends large enough to matter relative to the estimated effect.
- **Option (b): leads are diagnostic.** `std:13` applies only to the paper's substantive claims. For leads, it is enough that they are jointly insignificant and small in point estimate.
- **Option (c):** your own rule.

**`bs:T4`: `std:12` (symmetry) versus your contribution setting (a paper that denies what its audience takes for granted carries a higher burden of evidence).**
- **The pull.** The readership is dual. Economists and sociologists take different accounts for granted. A higher burden on denial makes the burden depend on which account the audience favours, and that is asymmetric between the accounts.
- **Option (a): symmetry governs the evidence.** The higher burden applies only to how strongly the paper may word its claims, which is already in `std:3` (e).
- **Option (b): the higher burden governs.** Then I need your rule for deciding what a dual audience takes for granted.
- **Option (c):** your own rule.

**`bs:T5`: `bs:EB.ann5` (one sentence on survival selection) versus `std:10` (comparison group, and differences before treatment; must).**
- **The pull.** If survival selection turns out to be a first-order threat to identification, `std:10` (c) and (d) would call for more than your self-imposed single sentence.
- **Option (a): the cap holds.** One sentence, in deference to the editor's settled item.
- **Option (b): `std:10` governs if the threat is first-order.** You add a short note to the editor explaining why you went past the cap. Mode C would check that the note is there.

**`bs:T6`: A clarification rather than a tension (priority versus weight).**
- Several must standards sit on dimensions with lower weights: `std:15` on PRA (0.4), and `std:5`, `std:6` and `std:9` on TEC (0.7).
- My reading: "must" means the standard must be applied in the draft, and the weight says how much a failure on that dimension moves the recommendation.
- On that reading, a failed TEC check would move the recommendation only when you say it "signals something deeper", as in your note on the TEC weight.
- You also said that over-claiming falls under INF and EPI. So the wording clauses in `std:2` (a) and `std:3` (e) carry the 0.9 weights, not PRA's 0.4.
- Please confirm or correct this reading. Mode C's consistency check depends on it.

##### 4. Is anything important missing?

The list stands at 16. Several of your Round 2 settings are themselves checkable, but Mode C checks standards, not settings. If you want any of the following checked in your draft, promote it to a standard and say which standard to merge or drop to make room. Or tell me you want the list to grow past 16.
- **Specification choice** (from EPI.5): the paper says how its main specification was chosen and reports the specifications that didn't work.
- **Adoption versus use** (from MI4): a paper that measures adoption and theorises about use argues for the link.
- **Assimilative reinterpretation** (from INF.6): reinterpreting the rival's evidence as the paper's own counts only if it yields a prediction the original reading does not.
- **Functional explanation** (from ONT.5): "it exists because it serves a function" needs a selection or feedback mechanism.
- **No "as if" defence** (from EPI.1): none for the assumption that does the work in a model.
- **Alternative safeguards** (from MI1): where a paper treats in-house governance as the remedy for hold-up, it considers the other safeguards, such as long-term contracts and hostages.

Beyond these: is there a check you perform that none of the 16 standards or the settings captures?

##### 5. How to reply

Short answers are fine. For example: "std:1–16 confirmed except std:6 (see Q2) · Q1 yes · T1 b · T2 a · … · promote: specification choice, merge into std:13".

**Decisions for the reviewer**
- Confirm or rewrite the checkable form of each of `std:1` to `std:16`.
- Answer the sharpening questions `bs:Q1` to `bs:Q8`.
- Rank or resolve tensions `bs:T1` to `bs:T5`, and confirm or correct the reading in `bs:T6`.
- Decide whether to promote any setting to a standard, and if so, what to merge or drop.
- Say whether anything important is missing.
- Correct anything in section 1 that I have recorded wrongly.

## `runs/01_dialogue/turn_08_reviewer_S3.md`

**Focal reviewer: reply to Mode S, Round 3 (`bs:S3`)** (Reviewership v0.1)

I still have not read the manuscript.

**The editor's own answers.** I'm told the protocol gives the reviewer the brief, not the editor's full answers, so my request is declined. Fine. I'll work from `bs:EB` and treat what it says about the manuscript as the editor's report, unchecked.

##### 0. One rule for every "Applied when"

My draft is about 1,000 words, written in a sitting of about an hour. As written, the "Applied when" clauses ask for a verdict on every condition for every item. That is a 4,000-word review. My rule:
- **Failures in the body.** The body of the draft states each condition that fails, where it fails, and what follows.
- **Passes in a list.** Passes go in a short "Checks run" list at the end, outside the 1,000 words and under 150 words. It says which standards I applied, to which items, and that they passed.
- **Missing inputs.** If I can't run a check because the paper doesn't report what it needs (descriptives, a correlation matrix, the covariances for a marginal effect), the draft asks for it. That counts as applied.

Mode C should count a standard as applied when either the body or the "Checks run" list shows it.

As I understand the protocol, I draft without the workbench's other capabilities. So no harness checks appear in the draft (see `bs:Q1`).

##### 1. Corrections to what you recorded

Section 1 is right, with one exception:
- **PRA.2.** Change it as I set out under `bs:T4` below. The higher burden attaches to the form of a claim ("rules out", "overturns"), whichever account the claim targets, not to what an audience takes for granted.

I agree on the citations: recollection is not verification.

##### 2. The 16 standards

I confirm the checkable form of each standard except where I say otherwise.

**`std:1`. Rewrite (b).**
- (b) "Defended" means argued to be true of the setting. For the assumption that does the work, convenience doesn't count, and neither does an "as if" defence. (This promotes the EPI.1 setting.)

**`std:2`. Rewrite (d); add (e).**
- (d) Add at the end: "...tested on evidence other than the failure the mechanism was introduced to explain."
- (e) A prediction fails when either of two things holds:
  - the estimate has the opposite sign, and its interval excludes zero; or
  - the interval rules out any effect in the predicted direction that is large enough to matter (as in `std:13`).

  An estimate that is merely imprecise is reported as "not supported", not as a failure, and the paper says which it is. The same definition applies to the rival's predictions (`std:12`).

**`std:3`. Confirm (a), (b), (d) and (e); (c) as under `bs:T2`; add (f) and (g).**
- (f) Reinterpreting the rival's evidence as the paper's own counts only if the reinterpretation yields a prediction that the rival's reading does not. (This promotes INF.6, the assimilative case.)
- (g) The same discipline applies to the paper's own mechanism, measured against the obvious non-rival explanations of the same correlation. The paper reports at least one implication specific to its mechanism, not only the reduced-form association. (g) is at should priority within this must standard.

**`std:4`. Confirm; define "addressed".** "Addressed" means tested, or given a specific reason why it doesn't apply. Listing it as a limitation doesn't count.

**`std:5`. Confirm (a) and (b); (c) as under `bs:Q1`.**

**`std:6`. Confirm; the minimum check is as under `bs:Q2`.**

**`std:7`. Confirm; add (d) and (e).**
- (d) The regressor and the outcome are not built from shared components, such as a common denominator or the same survey item, that would correlate them by construction.
- (e) Where a measure records adoption and the theory is about use, the paper argues the link between them. (This promotes MI4.)

**`std:8`. Confirm; add one clause; see `bs:Q4`.**
- Added clause: a claim that a practice exists because it serves a function names the selection or feedback mechanism. (This promotes ONT.5.)

**`std:9`. Confirm, including your definition of key regressors (which covers the rival's measure); add (c); see `bs:Q5`.**
- (c) Where key regressors vary at different levels, the paper clusters at the coarsest level, uses two-way clustering, or explains why not.

**`std:10`. Confirm (a), (b) and (d); (c), (e) and (f) as under `bs:T3`; add (g).**
- (g) The paper says how it chose the main specification and reports the specifications that didn't work. (This promotes EPI.5.)

The two citations in (e) match my memory: Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021), both in the *Journal of Econometrics*. Keep "to verify".

**`std:11`. Confirm; see `bs:Q6`.**

**`std:12`. Confirm; add (d).**
- (d) Wording cuts both ways. Any claim strength the draft rejects in statements about the rival ("ruled out", "fashion"), it also checks in statements about the paper's own account ("economizing", "shows"). See `bs:Q4`.

**`std:13`. Confirm; add to (a); see `bs:Q7`.**
- Added to (a): if I think the standard errors are clustered wrongly (`std:9`), I say that the interval is probably too narrow.

**`std:14`. Confirm; sharpen (a).**

I know the brief reports a lagged peer measure in this paper. I'd say the same of any lagged peer measure; it is a standard point in the peer-effects literature. I keep the sentence.
